title: Queues: enqueue, dequeue, front/rear and circular queues
learningObjectives: Explain the topic and its C rules.
Trace the example and explain its data or control flow.
Identify edge cases and resource-management requirements.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: A queue follows first-in, first-out order. A circular array queue reuses freed positions by wrapping indices around the capacity. A count or carefully managed front/rear state distinguishes empty and full conditions.
understand.whyItMatters: Queues support scheduling, buffering and breadth-first traversal. Circular storage avoids shifting every element after a dequeue.
understand.analogy: Treat each algorithm or resource as a contract whose invariants must remain true after every operation.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal rules for pointers, object lifetime, complexity or library contracts.

explain.narrative:
A queue follows first-in, first-out order. A circular array queue reuses freed positions by wrapping indices around the capacity. A count or carefully managed front/rear state distinguishes empty and full conditions.

State preconditions, invariants, empty and full cases, ownership and failure behaviour before implementation. Compile with warnings and test normal, boundary and failure paths.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: rear is calculated modulo capacity so it wraps to the beginning. The count field distinguishes full from empty even when front and rear indices coincide.

practise.guidedTask: Trace front and count through enqueue and dequeue operations.
practise.independentTask: Implement dequeue and peek, then test empty, full and wrap-around cases.
hints: Never apply modulo by a zero capacity.
Update count only after a successful queue operation.
Document whether the queue stores values or owns pointers to separately allocated objects.
